answer.label: Not Confucius — actually Atwood H. Townsend
answer.authorDates: born 1897 · NYU English professor & editor of “Good Reading”
answer.sourceLine: This is a 20th-century line about the value of reading, credited by Wikiquote ↗ to Atwood H. Townsend, editor of the guide Good Reading (various editions from at least 1960). It is not found in the Analects or any Confucian classic; the Confucius label is a modern quote-site fabrication.

source.excerpt: No matter how busy you may think you are, you must find time for reading, or surrender yourself to self-chosen ignorance.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Confucius Misattributed section (“Not Chinese”) and assigns it to Atwood H. Townsend, editor of Good Reading.
Quote-aggregator pages such as Goodreads ↗ reproduce the exact wording under Confucius’s name — an unverified, community-added attribution.
The wording appears in no Confucian classic; its documented home is Townsend’s Good Reading, a guide first assembled at NYU and reprinted in Mentor paperbacks.
source.excerptNote: Attached to Townsend’s reading guide, this reads as exactly what it is — a mid-century librarian’s exhortation to keep reading — not the compressed, aphoristic style of the Analects.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Atwood H. Townsend / New American Library (Mentor Books)
source.rightsNote: The line’s documented source, Townsend’s Good Reading, is a 20th-century work (editions from at least 1960, with origins in a 1941 NYU reading survey) — well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so it is treated as in-copyright to Townsend’s estate and its Mentor/New American Library publisher. The words are not from any public-domain Confucian text.

author.metaLine: born 1897 · New York University English professor & editor of Good Reading
author.bio: Atwood H. Townsend (born 1897) was a professor of English at the New York University School of Engineering who in the 1930s chaired the National Council of Teachers of English committee on college reading. He is best remembered as editor of Good Reading, a popular mid-century guide to worthwhile books that ran through many Mentor paperback editions.

misattribution.heading: Why Confucius gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Confucius is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for unsourced “wisdom” quotes. Any dignified, improving line — especially about learning — tends to drift onto his name, and this reading-advocacy sentence is a textbook case.

items.why: Countless quote sites and image memes print this under Confucius’s name, but Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed — Not Chinese. It is absent from the Analects and the other Confucian classics.
Wikiquote credits Townsend, editor of the reading guide Good Reading (various editions from at least 1960). The sentence is an editor’s pitch for the reading life, not an ancient Chinese aphorism.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: not Confucius. Per Wikiquote ↗, the line belongs to Atwood H. Townsend and his 20th-century guide Good Reading.

context.heading: A librarian’s slogan, not a sage’s maxim
lead: The sentence does real rhetorical work for a reading guide: it flatters the busy reader, then warns that skipping books is a self-inflicted “self-chosen ignorance.” That is the voice of a mid-century book-list editor selling the habit of reading — which is precisely what Townsend’s Good Reading was for.

Confucius, by contrast, survives to us in the terse, dialogic form of the Analects. The polished English abstraction here — and the total absence of the line from any Confucian text — is the tell that it is modern.
context.pull: “Self-chosen ignorance” is a book-guide editor’s pitch, not a line from the Analects.
